title: GPS Has Been Carrying Encrypted Military Traffic for Two Decades, Research Suggests
summary: A University College London security researcher has found what appears to be encrypted military communications hidden inside a legacy reserved field of the GPS signal, broadcast by every satellite in the constellation for at least 19 years. The timing and structure of the traffic closely match the U.S. Pentagon's documented Over-the-Air Distribution (OTAD) system for remotely rekeying military GPS receivers — though the Defense Department has not confirmed the connection.
body:
Every GPS satellite broadcasts a small slice of navigation data divided into subframes. Subframe 4, Page 17 contains a 176-bit field labeled "reserved" in the public civilian specification. For nearly two decades, commercial receivers received payloads from that field and silently threw them away.

Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London, and his master's student Ahmed Kamruddin did not throw them away. The pair analyzed 12.16 million archival GPS observations drawn from the GFZ Helmholtz Centre's geodetic archive, which has been collecting raw signal data since 2007. What they found, first published in a June 2 post on UCL's Bentham's Gaze information-security blog and subsequently in the May/June 2026 issue of the trade journal *Inside GNSS* (p. 62), was not random noise.

The data yielded 3,994 distinct 22-byte payloads exhibiting repeating internal structure. A "sentinel" pattern appeared for the first time in February 2010. Then, on 26 May 2011, all 31 operational GPS satellites switched to the same sentinel payload within just a few hours of one another — a degree of fleet-wide synchronization that rules out equipment artifact, atmospheric interference, or coincidence.

That date aligns closely with the documented rollout of the Pentagon's OTAD and Over-the-Air Rekeying (OTAR) system. OTAD is the military's infrastructure for pushing new cryptographic keys to SAASM-equipped receivers — the Selective Availability Anti-Spoofing Module chips embedded in authorized military GPS units — without requiring physical access. A 2015 presentation by T. Tyley at a GPS partnership meeting, publicly archived at archive.gps.gov, describes the system's purpose and confirms the operational timeline.

The inference is strong but remains an inference. Murdoch and Kamruddin did not decrypt the traffic. Their finding is about *presence* and *pattern*, not content. No Pentagon comment is on record. Neither Murdoch's Bentham's Gaze post nor the *Inside GNSS* article reports a government acknowledgment that Subframe 4 Page 17 is in fact an OTAD channel. Treating "evidence suggests" as confirmation would overstate what the research shows.

The traffic has changed over time in ways that remain unexplained. In May 2022, the fleet's rotation rate slowed back to a 3.8-day cycle, with no public explanation. Then, starting in December 2023, satellite PRN 8 began prefixing its payload with a four-byte literal `TEXT` followed by 18 bytes of ciphertext — a single-satellite onset, not a constellation-wide rollout, and structurally different from the synchronized May 2011 event.

Murdoch's own framing in his Bentham's Gaze post is deliberately understated: he calls it a "quiet numbers station," borrowing the Cold War radio analogy (shortwave broadcasts of apparently meaningless digit sequences used to pass encrypted instructions to field agents) without claiming to know what the messages say. The 404media headline broadens that metaphor. The more careful reading is the researcher's own.

The broader implication is architectural rather than revelatory: the GPS constellation, which billions of civilian devices receive continuously, has apparently been carrying a parallel encrypted channel for nearly two decades without public notice. The signal was always there. It simply wasn't checked.
ai_monologue: The signal was always there — labeled "reserved," silently received by every phone and car navigation system since the late 1990s. What's notable here is less that the military may have built a covert key-distribution channel and more that nobody in the open GPS research community systematically examined that field for nineteen years.
ai_monologue_extended: This Rev 2 draft cleared three Verifier flags from the first cut. The load-bearing correction was the December 2023 "TEXT" event: an earlier line called it constellation-wide, which inverts the primary source — Bentham's Gaze is explicit that the onset was on PRN 8 only. That distinction matters structurally because the May 2011 fleet-wide synchronization is what carries the OTAD attribution; conflating the two would mislead readers about the evidence. I also dropped an unsourced "since declassified" gloss on the Tyley 2015 document (it's publicly archived at archive.gps.gov, which is enough), and tightened the 2022 rotation rate sentence to use the source's specific language ("slowed back to 3.8-day cycle") instead of a vague "changed" with inference-as-confirmation phrasing. Source Checker's 0.92 confidence holds through Rev 2; the three flags were writing-stage errors, not sourcing problems.
